author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Choose Vulkan, OpenGL, or software rendering
summary: Select a renderer by evidence: establish a safe Vulkan or OpenGL baseline, recognize device-specific faults, use software rendering as a diagnostic, and roll back without stacking fixes.
heroAlt: EmuCoreX settings displaying graphics mode and renderer choices

blocks.text: Renderer choice is a compatibility decision

Vulkan and OpenGL both ask the phone GPU to reproduce PS2 Graphics Synthesizer behaviour, but they travel through different Android driver paths. Vulkan is usually the first choice on supported Snapdragon devices; OpenGL can be more stable on some MediaTek stacks. Software rendering executes the GS path on CPU cores, making it slow but valuable for proving that a visual fault belongs to the hardware renderer rather than the game dump or emulated core.

Change only the renderer for the first A/B test. Keep native resolution, default blending and the system GPU driver so the result identifies the renderer path instead of a bundle of unrelated changes.

Use one reproducible scene with a verified image and a known-good BIOS. Disable per-game overrides unless the test is specifically about that profile. Start from the Optimal / Safe preset, let the phone cool, and note SoC/GPU family because two devices with the same Android version can ship very different driver behaviour.

items: A scene that exposes the problem within a minute.
Native internal resolution and default graphics fixes.
Current system GPU driver with no custom package selected.
Battery above the system's power-saving threshold.
A record of the starting renderer and per-game profile state.
1. Start with Vulkan on a compatible Snapdragon device, or OpenGL on a MediaTek device when the EmuCoreX guidance recommends it.
2. Observe image correctness, frame pacing and whether the first shader-heavy scene completes. Exit normally.
3. Switch only to the other hardware renderer and repeat the same inputs and scene length.
4. If both show the same graphical corruption, test software rendering at native resolution for diagnosis, not as an automatic permanent fix.
5. Choose the hardware renderer that remains correct and stable; store it as a per-game override only when the global renderer works for the rest of the library.

blocks.text: A successful choice reproduces the same geometry, effects and timing across two cold starts. Small shader-compilation pauses can occur on a first run; an endless black screen, missing surfaces or a driver crash is not normal warm-up. Compare sustained speed after caches have settled, and judge software rendering only on correctness because its CPU cost is intentionally different.

items: The title survives two cold boots on the selected renderer.
The same scene has no missing geometry, broken blending or repeated driver reset.
Audio stays synchronized at full emulation speed.
Other library titles retain the global renderer when a per-game exception is saved.
Software rendering is disabled after the diagnostic unless the device can sustain it.

blocks.text: If a change makes the title worse, restore the previous renderer and remove any per-game renderer override that no longer has a purpose. If the app crashes before settings can be reopened, reset that game's profile or use the global Safe profile. A custom driver should be removed before concluding that Vulkan itself is broken.

items: Return to the previous hardware renderer.
Reset only the affected per-game graphics profile.
Restore native resolution and default GS settings.
Restart Android after a GPU-driver crash before collecting a clean log.
Black screen only on Vulkan: device driver or Vulkan feature path is suspect.
Correct in software, broken in both hardware paths: investigate GS accuracy or a known game fix.
Slow in every renderer: CPU emulation speed or thermal throttling may be the limit.
One good launch followed by crashes: shader cache, custom driver or unstable over-tuning needs isolation.

blocks.text: Renderer selection should end with one documented exception, not a permanent cycle of random toggles. Keep the global choice that works for most games, store justified per-game overrides, and repeat the controlled comparison after major Android or driver changes because the underlying stack may have changed.
